newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus president leaves for OSCE summit.
newsitem.headline: Belarus president leaves for OSCE summit.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko of Belarus, who won sweeping new powers in a controversial referendum last week, left on Sunday for a European security summit in Portugal.

But Lukashenko, who sent police to close down parliament on Thursday after winning powers to reshape state institutions, said on Belarussian television he expected the summit to be concerned mainly about NATO and European security.
"I must say it will be a very difficult summit because there will be very many disagreements concerning NATO and European states," he said on the steps of his plane.
"Europe has been looking forward to becoming independent as far as its security is concerned. The United States and its supporters do not like that aim," he said.
Belarus occupies a strategically important position, bordering Russia, Poland, Ukraine, Latvia and Lithuania.
Russia and Belarus marked the withdrawal of the last Soviet nuclear missile from Belarussian soil last Wednesday and reiterated their strong opposition to NATO's eastward expansion.

"We have withdrawn from our territory the last missile at the request of our partners. Certainly we will demand relevant guarantees from our neighbours, European states and the United States," Lukashenko said on Sunday.

Diplomats in the West have said Lukashenko can expect protests at the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) meeting in Lisbon over his authoritarian rule and attempts to secure more powers.
The European Uunion said last week it was seriously concerned about events in the former Soviet republic of 10 million people.

After winning more than 70 percent support in the referendum, Lukashenko signed a new constitution which a delegation from the Council of Europe human rights forum said "fell short of minimum democratic standards".
Deputies supporting the president abolished the old parliament.
The OSCE could vote to suspend Belarussian membership if all other members agree. But diplomats said this was unlikely as many nations wanted to try to resolve the problem with dialogue.
